## Customisable ecosystem summary heatmaps

```{r setup}
load_all()    # for developer
# library(pacea)  # for user
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)  # Else prints all of a tibble
library(ggplot2)
```

In the
[buoy_anomalies](https://pbs-assess.github.io/pacea/vignettes/buoy_anomalies.html)
vignette we showed how to make customisable heatmaps of the buoy sea-surface
temperature data that are saved in pacea. They are in a format famililar to
oceanographers, using prescribed climatologies and subsequent anomalies.

Here we show how to produce customisable heatmaps that include disparate types
of ecosystem information, thus bringing together the various data objects in
pacea. Importantly the user can choose:

- the types of ecosystem information to be included, tailored to their
  particular stock;
- the area over which spatial information is summarised.

The aim of pacea is to
facilitate inclusion of ecosystem information in advice to fisheries management,
such as stock assessments. Given the multitude of stocks in DFO's Pacific
Region, both in terms of the diversity of species and the many stock-specific spatial areas, we decided
to create functions for user-customisable plots that easily summarise the relevant ecosystem
information.

Expert knowledge can be used to suggest relevant ecosystem information to be
used for a particular stock. Futhermore, the ease of generating the heatmaps can
allow exploration, formulation of ideas, and quick hypothesis testing.

For comparing disparate types of ecosystem information, we calculate an annual
index which is standardised (by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation across
the time series; note that all years might not get shown in a plot).
This is so that indices
are all dimensionless and can be compared on equivalent scales, and shown on a
single heatmap style plot.

As a general proof-of-concept example, let's use some ecosystem information for the Strait of Georgia
(SOG) that is in pacea. We create an index for each type of ecosystem information in turn and
then make the plot. We just need to use `create_index()` multiple times to
create the indices, and then `plot_indices()` to make the function (we will
explain the functions in more detail later):
```{r, examples}
# Average sea surface temperature in April from a buoy in the SOG
sst_buoy_halibut_bank_apr_index <- create_index(buoy_sst,
                                                months = 4,
                                                stn_id = "Halibut Bank")

# Large calanoid copepods in the SOG 
calanoid_copepods_large_sog_index <- create_index(zooplankton_sog,
                                                  zooplankton_species_group =
                                                    "calanoid_copepods_large")

# Total zooplankton in the SOG
total_zooplankton_sog_index <- create_index(zooplankton_sog,
                                            zooplankton_species_group = "total_biomass")

# Annual age-2 herring recruitment in the SOG
herring_recruitment_sog_index <- create_index(herring_recruitment,
                                              herring_region = "SOG")

# Annual herring spawning biomass in the SOG
herring_biomass_sog_index <- create_index(herring_spawning_biomass,
                                          herring_region = "SOG")

# Annual population estimates of Harbour Seals in the SOG
harbour_seals_sog_index <- create_index(harbour_seals,
                                        seal_region = "SOG")
```
See the
relevant vignettes and help files for details of the pacea objects used for each
index. The first index is from the buoy sea surface temperature. Looking at the [buoy_anomalies](https://pbs-assess.github.io/pacea/vignettes/buoy_anomalies.html)
vignette we have used the Halibut Bank buoy in the SoG, which has good timespans of
data, and just pick April. 

The `create_index()` function automatically creates an object of class
`pacea_standardised_index`, no matter what type the ecosystem information is. 

Now make the plot, manually basing the start year on the shortest
of those (zooplankton data):
```{r, sogplot, fig.height = fig_height_five_row_heatmap}
plot_indices(sst_buoy_halibut_bank_apr_index,
             calanoid_copepods_large_sog_index,
             total_zooplankton_sog_index,
             herring_recruitment_sog_index,
             herring_biomass_sog_index,             
             harbour_seals_sog_index,
             years = 1996:2026,
             gap_after = c("sst_buoy_halibut_bank_apr_index",
                           "total_zooplankton_sog_index",
                           "herring_biomass_sog_index"))
```

The first six arguments are the indices that we created above, and `years`
restricts the plot to the years specified.
To delineate different types of ecosystem information in the plot
(e.g. here we have temperature, zooplankton, fish, mammals), we used the optional
`gap_after` argument to add a small gap after the specified indices.

Each index is standardised over its full time series, and red for a year indicates
above-average conditions, blue indicates below-average, with the black numbers
giving the exact standardised anomaly (number of standard deviations above the
mean), as used for the colour coding. 

The restriction of the years being shown is why the seal index is always
positive. By definition the mean of an index across its full time series 
is 0, and so the seal index must be negative earlier in the time series. A quick check of
the absolute seal populations numbers confirms this, in that the  population has
indeed 
increased from the early years:

```{r, sealplot, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4}
plot(harbour_seals,
     region = "SOG")
```

Here are the details of what is in the buoy SST index object created above:
```{r, indexdetails}
sst_buoy_halibut_bank_apr_index
```
It is a tibble, with a value for each year, plus an `index` to refer to in code,
and an `index_label` to use for the labels in the plot (these are repeated in
each row, which just makes things easier at the plotting stage). 

We can also choose multiple months. Note that `index` and `index_label`
get automatically prescribed;
examine the arguments and results for these three indices (for the default buoy,
namely that 
in West Dixon Entrance):
```{r, createindmonths}
create_index(buoy_sst,
             months = 5)
create_index(buoy_sst,
             months = 5:6)
create_index(buoy_sst,
             months = c(11, 12, 1, 2, 3))
```
In the third example note how the months are specified from November to March -
the year indicated is the year of the January.

Note that in the first example we have a value for 1992, but not in the second
one. This must be because June 1992 does not have enough daily values for this
particular buoy, which we can confirm from the raw data:
```{r, confirm}
filter(buoy_sst,
       stn_id == "C46205",   # default in create_index.pacea_buoy()
       date >= "1992-06-01",
       date <= "1992-06-30",
       !is.na(sst))
```
So there are only 6 daily SST values for this buoy in June 1992, and so an
anomaly is not calculated for that month because the default is to require 15
daily SST values in a month. We could force an anomaly to be
calculated by changing the arguments `min_days_per_month` (default 15) and 
`max_consecutive_missing_days` (default 6) that get passed onto
`calculate_anomalies.pacea_buoy()`:
```{r, confirmchange}
create_index(buoy_sst,
             months = 5:6,
             min_days_per_month = 6,
             max_consecutive_missing_days = 24)
```
thus giving an index value for 1992, given these definitions (which we do not
recommend, but are showing as examples to help understanding, and to show that
arguments get correctly passed onto further functions). 

For any type of pacea object, check the exact calculations and further options
by checking `class(object)` and then `?create_index.<class>`. For example
`?create_index.pacea_buoy` for the `buoy_sst` data.


## OISST spatiotemporal data

We now create various indices from the Optimally Interpolated Sea Surface
Temperature (OISST) spatiotemporal data, that are described in
[oisst.html](https://pbs-assess.github.io/pacea/vignettes/oisst.html). 
An index is a single standardised value
for each year, and for SST would be based on the mean anomalies over a given
area.

It is first best to plot the spatial anomalies for the area of interest, to
verify the area and understand what is going on. We wil then calculate an index
directly from the anomalies list, or 
directly from `create_index(oisst_month)` with various options.

First, let's look at the full domain of the OISST data and calculate annual
anomalies and do the default plot (which is for the most recent month of data):
```{r, oisst1, fig.height = fig_height_one_map}
oisst_anomalies <- calculate_anomalies(oisst_month)

plot(oisst_anomalies)
```

The `oisst_anomalies` list object (of class `pacea_oisst_anomalies_list`) contains the climatology for each month-location
combination, plus the anomalies relative to those for each year-month-location
combination, plus the `climatology_years` used:
```{r, oisst3}
oisst_anomalies
```

We can specify months and years in a plot, chosen here to show the marine heatwave forming
in 2014:
```{r, oisst2, fig.height = fig_height_three_map}
plot(oisst_anomalies,
     months = 1:12,
     years = 2014:2016,
     x_axis_labels = c(-135, -125)) # specify the x-axis labels to be shown     
```

We can create an index of the mean anomaly each year averaged over, say, Apr-Jun, over the
full domain shown (which is Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone):

```{r, fulldomain}
oisst_eez_apr_jun_index <- create_index(oisst_anomalies,
                                        months = 4:6,
                                        index_name =
                                          "oisst_apr_to_jun_over_eez",
                                        index_label = "OISST for Apr to Jun over EEZ")
oisst_eez_apr_jun_index
```
The index tibble has the same format as the other types shown above, with one
value per day. We can simply add this to our earlier heatmap summary plot:
```{r, sogplot2, fig.height = fig_height_six_row_heatmap}
plot_indices(oisst_eez_apr_jun_index,
             sst_buoy_halibut_bank_apr_index,
             calanoid_copepods_large_sog_index,
             total_zooplankton_sog_index,
             herring_recruitment_sog_index,
             herring_biomass_sog_index,             
             harbour_seals_sog_index,
             years = 1996:2026,
             gap_after = c("sst_buoy_halibut_bank_apr_index",
                           "total_zooplankton_sog_index",
                           "herring_biomass_sog_index"))
```
This is showing the proof of concept, in that, we can easily compare the
mean SST anomaly across the whole EEZ over April to June with the buoy SST mean
anomaly for April, at one location (the point being you can define an index
however you like and easily compare it). 

In practice, we likely want to restrict an index (and annual summary figure) to a
specific spatial region, and also specific months.

### Restricting an index over a spatial area

To create anomalies for a specific area, such as Pacific Marine
Fisheries Area 126, again showing
the heatwave progressing
```{r, area126plot, fig.height = fig_height_three_map}
oisst_anomalies_area_126 <- calculate_anomalies(oisst_month,
                                                area = pfma_area_126_temp)

plot(oisst_anomalies_area_126,
     months = 1:12,
     years = 2014:2016,
     restrict_plot = TRUE,          # restrict the plot to the area of the anomalies
     buffer_proportion = 0.6,       # add a buffer proportion to zoom out a bit
     x_axis_labels = c(-130, -128)) # specify the x-axis labels to be shown
```
(Some of those settings are hard to automate with multiple panels, so users may need to
tweak the options; also `pfma_area_126_temp` is a temporary data object in pacea
and will change names when we import many fisheries management areas).

For investigating plots (rather than doing analyses), we can also simply use the `area`
argument when plotting the full `oisst_anomalies`, giving the same plot as above
(so we have not shown it again here):
```{r, area126inplot, eval = FALSE}
plot(oisst_anomalies,
     area = pfma_area_126_temp,
     months = 1:12,
     years = 2014:2016,
     restrict_plot = TRUE,
     buffer_proportion = 0.6,
     x_axis_labels = c(-130, -128))
```

To calculate the index for Area 126 in April (the default), and give it an appropriate name and label:
```{r, oisstindex}
oisst_area_126_apr_index <- create_index(oisst_anomalies_area_126,
                                         index_name = "oisst_apr_area_126",
                                         index_label = "OISST in Apr over Area 126")   # April is the default

oisst_area_126_apr_index
```
For comparison we can also calculate the mean sea surface temperature for April from a buoy
within area 126
```{r, buoy126, fig.height = fig_height_two_row_heatmap}
sst_buoy_south_brooks_apr_index <- create_index(buoy_sst,
                                                months = 4,
                                                stn_id = "South Brooks")
plot_indices(oisst_area_126_apr_index,
             sst_buoy_south_brooks_apr_index)
```
This shows that the two different indices representing SST are fairly correlated
but not exactly the same, as expected.

<!-- TODO phase plot when done -->

It makes sense to restrict the plot to 1995 onwards when we have both types of
data. You can either restrict the years in the plot, or recalculate the OISST
anomalies from 1995 onwards. Note how these give slightly different figures;
restricting the plot:
```{r, buoy126b, fig.height = fig_height_two_row_heatmap}
plot_indices(oisst_area_126_apr_index,
             sst_buoy_south_brooks_apr_index,
             years = 1995:2026)
```
or recalculate a restricted index:
```{r, buoy126c, fig.height = fig_height_two_row_heatmap}
oisst_area_126_apr_from_1995_index <-
  create_index(oisst_anomalies_area_126,
               years = 1995:2026)

plot_indices(oisst_area_126_apr_from_1995_index,
             sst_buoy_south_brooks_apr_index)
```

You can also create an index directly from the `oisst_month` data, for which the
anomalies are calculated internally. Though it seems better to calculate
the full spatial anomalies for your area to take a look at them first, as we did
above. Nevertheless, `create_index()` will work directly on `oisst_month`, with
the `area` option, giving the same result as above
```{r, oisstindex2}
oisst_area_126_apr_index_directly <- create_index(oisst_month,
                                                  area = pfma_area_126_temp,
                                                  index_name =
                                                    "oisst_apr_area_126",
                                                  index_label = "OISST in Apr over Area 126")

expect_equal(oisst_area_126_apr_index,
             oisst_area_126_apr_index_directly)
```

We can also show every month of a spatially averaged anomaly in a heatmap style
plot, like in the
[buoy_anomalies](https://pbs-assess.github.io/pacea/vignettes/buoy_anomalies.html)
vignette. This nicely summarises the many spatial maps (which can't all easily
digested by a reader) into one plot. Note that these are NOT annual indices:

```{r, oisstheatmap}
plot(oisst_anomalies_area_126,
     heatmap_style = TRUE,
     area_name = "Area 126")
```

You can just do a few months of interest:
```{r, oisstheatmap2, fig.height = fig_height_three_row_heatmap}
plot(oisst_anomalies_area_126,
     heatmap_style = TRUE,
     area_name = "Area 126",
     months = 3:5)
```

See the code of the vignette (specifically the chunk headers) to see how to get
the figure sizes looking good; these are not automated in the functions.

If you have read this far then you deserve to learn about another, lesser known,
spatial area available in pacea.

```{r, anomaliessqtch, fig.height = fig_height_three_map}
oisst_anomalies_sasquatch <- calculate_anomalies(oisst_month,
                                                 area = sasquatch)

plot(oisst_anomalies_sasquatch,
     restrict_plot = TRUE,
     buffer_proportion = 1,
     area_outline = sasquatch)
```

In average years, the sasquatch appears to hide away, only coming out when it's warm or cold:
```{r, anomaliessqtchmap, fig.height = fig_height_four_map}
plot(oisst_anomalies_sasquatch,
     months = 4,
     years = 2014:2026)
```

And we can create a new index, and see how it compares to that above for Area 126:
```{r, sasindex, fig.height = fig_height_two_row_heatmap}
oisst_sasquatch_apr_index <- create_index(oisst_anomalies_sasquatch,
                                months = 4,
                                index_label = "OISST in Sasquatch for Apr")

plot_indices(oisst_sasquatch_apr_index,
             oisst_area_126_apr_index)
```

## Climatological and oceanographic indices

For details of the climatological and oceanographic indices available in pacea
see the [indices](https://pbs-assess.github.io/pacea/vignettes/indices.html)
vignette. For example, we have developed a heatmap style that is particularly
useful for understanding the emergence of El Niño (see vignette for more
details), with shades of blue representing La Niña conditions, grey representing
neutral, and shades of red representing El Niño:

```{r, oniheatmap}
plot(oni,
     years = 1980:2026,
     neutral_oni_one_colour = TRUE,
     heatmap_style = TRUE)
```

We can create an index based on a few months of ONI, let's say Nov-Jan, based on
the above figure:
```{r, onindexnovjan}
oni_index_nov_jan <- create_index(oni,
                                  months = c(11, 12, 1))
```

We can see if that looks to correlate with the previously calculated index of
temperature in Area 126, off the west coast of Vancouver Island:

```{r, oni126, fig.height = fig_height_two_row_heatmap}
plot_indices(oni_index_nov_jan,
             oisst_area_126_apr_index,
             years = 1982:2026)             
```
(Note that the standardised ONI here is standardised like all variables in
such a plot, as noted in the
title, so values are not
the same as for usually-defined ONI).

The red and blues generally match up, although there are
some exceptions. The
correlation coefficient is
```{r, corr}
cor(filter(oni_index_nov_jan, year >= 1982)$value,
    oisst_area_126_apr_index$value) %>% round(2)
```

Interestingly, the averaged temperature over Area 126 (second row) for 2026 is 0.9 -- only
in 2025 and 2026 has it been >0.5 when the standardised ONI the previous Nov to
Jan is negative (blue). So coming into an El Niño for 2026-2027, the water is already
relatively warm. This shows the sort
of hypotheses you can start looking into and trying to understand. And because
we have the values available, we can make a quick plot to demonstrate this last
point:
```{r, onineg, fig.width = 7}
# Values of the standardised ONI that are negative:
oni_index_neg <- filter(oni_index_nov_jan,
                        year >= 1982,     # when OISST data start
                        value <= 0)
# Corresponding Area 126 April mean OISST for those years:
oisst_area_126_apr_oni_neg <- filter(oisst_area_126_apr_index,
                                     year %in% oni_index_neg$year)

plot(oisst_area_126_apr_oni_neg$year,
     oisst_area_126_apr_oni_neg$value,
     xlab = "Year",
     ylab = "OISST in April over Area 126",
     main = "Only for years with a negative standardised ONI")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey")
``` 

We can also look at potential correlations with the other temperature indices we
calculated above (for a buoy and for4 the whole EEZ):
```{r, onitemp, fig.height = fig_height_four_row_heatmap}
plot_indices(oni_index_nov_jan,
             oisst_area_126_apr_index,
             sst_buoy_south_brooks_apr_index,
			 oisst_sasquatch_apr_index,
             oisst_eez_apr_jun_index,
             years = 1982:2026,
             gap_after = c("oni_index_nov_jan",
                           "sst_buoy_south_brooks_apr_index"))
```

<!-- TODO add a phase plot when done. A simple correlation plot does not really -->
<!-- show this up, a phase plot with years might. The numbers force you to look -->
<!-- and think a bit-->

For the South Brooks buoy, 2026 is the only year with an anomaly of 0.5 and a
negative standardised ONI over the pevious Nov to Jan, except for 1996 (that had
a low standardised ONI value of -0.9).

For the full EEZ (bottom row), the signal is not as strong.

The earlier point above about ONI and Area 126 in 2025 and 2026
does not show really show up in a simple plot (the years in question are
highlighted in red, but otherwise would not really stand out; to be improved with a general
phase plot function):
```{r, oniarea126plot, fig.width = 5}
plot(filter(oni_index_nov_jan, year >= 1982)$value,
     oisst_area_126_apr_index$value,
     xlab = oni_index_nov_jan$index_label[1],
     ylab = oisst_area_126_apr_index$index_label[1])
points(filter(oni_index_nov_jan,
              year %in% 2025:2026)$value,
       filter(oisst_area_126_apr_index,
              year %in% 2025:2026)$value,
       col = "red")
```

This demonstrates the usefulness of the heatmap-style plot.

The `create_index()` function works on all the climatological and oceanographic indices in
pacea (PDO, NPGO, etc.; see `pacea_indices`) and so that plus `plot_indices()` could be used to
compare and help understand the relationships between the various indices. An exercise for the reader.

## Tailoring for a specific stock

In the [2025 Pacific Hake stock
assessment](https://s3.amazonaws.com/media.fisheries.noaa.gov/2025-02/Status-Pacific-Hake-whiting-US-and-Canadian-waters-2025.pdf)
we presented a hake-specific ecosystem summary as a first step to providing an
operational summary of relevant ecosystem information regarding the coastwide
Pacific Hake (from California to British Columbia). It was updated in the [2026
assessment](https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/s3/2026-02/hake-assessment-2026.pdf),
with about half of the information coming directly from pacea. 

Without going into too much detail (see the assessments), we now
develop an ecosystem summary heatmap of some of the ecosystem influences on Pacific Hake
recruitment (age-0 individuals). This  will improve upon the time-series style
plots used in the 2025 and 2026 assessments. 

We show five indices from pacea:


| Definition | Effect on recruitment | Expectation for an increase in the index |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Pacific Herring spawning biomass off the west coast of
Vancouver Island | Increased competition with herring on summer feeding grounds
leads to poorer feeding conditions and reduced adult condition |
$\downarrow$ recruitment the following year |

| North Pacific Current Bifurcation Index | Northward-shifted
bifurcation leads to increased advection of prey southwards, leading to poorer
feeding conditions off British Columbia, Washington, and Oregon, and reduced
adult condition | $\downarrow$ recruitment the following year |

| Pacific Decadal Oscillation during preconditioning (Apr-Sep) | Indicator of basin-scale
processes, negative phase linked to higher productivity and improved adult
condition (Apr-Sep) |
$\downarrow$ recruitment the following year |

| North Pacific Gyre Oscillation during preconditioning
(Apr-Sep) | Indicator of basin-scale
processes, positive phase linked to higher nutrient concentrations and
productivity, and improved adult condition | 
$\uparrow$ recruitment the following year |


We introduce two new options in `plot_indicces()`:

- lagging an index when the influence of the index is on the following
   year's hake recruitment;
- flipping the colour scale when a negative index is expected to positively
   enhance hake recruitment.
   
First we will create the relevant indices from pacea objects:
<!-- adapted from `ecosystem_summary_hake.R` -->
```{r, hake}
hake_assessment_year <- 2026
hake_recruitment_final_year_to_use <- 2022  # final years removed as not
            # estimated by data, depends on the model assumptions        
age_1_hake_final_year_to_use <- hake_recruitment_final_year_to_use + 1

hake_recruitment_index <- create_index(
  filter(hake_recruitment,
         year <= hake_recruitment_final_year_to_use),
  index_name = "hake_recruitment",
  index_label = "Pacific Hake age-0 recruitment")

hake_recruitment_index %>% tail()

start_year <- hake_recruitment_index$year[1]

herring_biomass_wcvi_index <- create_index(filter(herring_spawning_biomass,
                                                  year >= start_year),
                                           herring_region = "WCVI",
                                           index_name =
                                             "herring_spawning_biomass_wcvi")
bi_index <- create_index(bi,
                         index_label = "Bifurcation Index")


hake_age_1_index <- create_index(filter(hake_total_biomass_age_1,
                                        year <= age_1_hake_final_year_to_use),
                                 index_name = "hake_age_1_total_biomass",
                                 index_label = "Pacific Hake age-1 biomass")

pdo_index <- create_index(filter(pdo,
                                 year >= start_year),
                          months = 4:9,
                          index_name = "pdo_preconditioning",
                          index_label = "PDO Preconditioning")

npgo_index <- create_index(filter(npgo,
                                 year >= start_year),
                          months = 4:9,
                          index_name = "npgo_preconditioning",
                          index_label = "NPGO Preconditioning")

plot_indices(hake_recruitment_index,
             pdo_index,
             npgo_index,
             bi_index,             
             herring_biomass_wcvi_index,
             hake_age_1_index,
             years = 1995:2027,    # else a bit unwieldy
             gap_after = c("hake_recruitment_index",
                           "bi_index",
                           "herring_biomass_wcvi_index"),
             flip = c("pdo_index",
                      "bi_index",
                      "herring_biomass_wcvi_index",
                      "hake_age_1_index"),
             shift = c("pdo_index",
                       "npgo_index",
                       "bi_index",
                       "herring_biomass_wcvi_index")
             )                      
```
(Tried with and without log of hake recruitment and age-1's -- prefer unlogged
as it shows up the really big recruitments better, logged makes the very small
stand out compared to small, which is not so important. See commented out code.)

```{r, hakelog, eval = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
hake_recruitment_log <- hake_recruitment %>%
  mutate(median = log(median))

hake_recruitment_log_index <- create_index(
  filter(hake_recruitment_log,
         year <= hake_recruitment_final_year_to_use),
  index_name = "hake_recruitment_log",
  index_label = "Pacific Hake age-0 log recruitment")

hake_recruitment_log_index %>% tail()

# Using recruitment deviations gives very close numbers to log recruitment
#  (because of biomass lies close to the asymptote of the stock-recruit curve)
# hake_recruitment_deviations_index <- create_index(
#  filter(hake_recruitment_deviations,
#         year <= hake_recruitment_final_year_to_use),
#  index_name = "hake_recruitment_deviations",
# index_label = "Pacific Hake age-0 recruitment deviations")

hake_total_biomass_age_1_log <- hake_total_biomass_age_1 %>%
  mutate(median = log(median))

hake_age_1_log_index <- create_index(filter(hake_total_biomass_age_1_log,
                                            year <= age_1_hake_final_year_to_use),
                                     index_name = "hake_age_1_total_biomass_log",
                                     index_label = "Pacific Hake age-1 log biomass")


```

## Final remarks

Using our functions described above, you should be able to tailor ecosystem summary
heatmaps for your own stock or species of interest. We see these allowing you to
be exploratory, generate hypotheses, and
help you include ecosystem information when providing
advice to fisheries management.

<!-- 
A final example, though thing we have enough: does the ONI index the previous winter seem to relate to
herring recruitment across the five herring regions and hake recruitment (which
is mostly in US waters)? Also, how synchronous
is recruitment across those regions? 
-->
```{r, furtherexamples, fig.height = fig_height_six_row_heatmap, fig.width = 18, eval = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
pdo_annual_index <- create_index(pdo,
                          months = 1:12)
herring_recruitment_hg_index <- create_index(herring_recruitment,
                                             herring_region= "HG")
herring_recruitment_prd_index <- create_index(herring_recruitment,
                                              herring_region = "PRD")
herring_recruitment_cc_index <- create_index(herring_recruitment,
                                             herring_region = "CC")
herring_recruitment_wcvi_index <- create_index(herring_recruitment,
                                              herring_region = "WCVI")
hake_recruitment_index <- create_index(hake_recruitment)

# Many examples (adding as go along), likely not really needed:
plot_indices(pdo_annual_index,
             herring_recruitment_hg_index,
             herring_recruitment_prd_index,
             herring_recruitment_cc_index,
             herring_recruitment_sog_index,
             herring_recruitment_wcvi_index,
             hake_recruitment_index,
             years = 1953:2026,    # it ignores 2026 if no values though
             gap_after = c("pdo_annual_index",
                           "herring_recruitment_wcvi_index"))
```

```{r, updateoni2}
oni_new <- readr::read_table("oni.txt")

stopifnot(colnames(oni_new) == c("SEAS", "YR", "TOTAL", "ANOM"),
          oni_new[1, 1] == "DJF")    # If this fails then months as factors
                                     #  below will become incorrect because it
                                     #  assumes first one is January

colnames(oni_new)<-c("month",
                     "year",
                     "value",
                     "anomaly")

oni_new <- dplyr::relocate(oni_new,
                           year)

oni_new$month <- as.numeric(factor(oni_new$month,
                                   levels=unique(oni_new$month),
                                   ordered=TRUE))
class(oni_new) <- c("pacea_index",
                    class(oni_new))

attr(oni_new, "axis_name") <- "Oceanic Niño Index"

plot(oni_new,
     years = 1980:2026,
     neutral_oni_one_colour = TRUE,
     heatmap_style = TRUE)

```

